prompt:
Find the $n$th derivative of the function
$$f(x)=\frac{x}{x^2-1}.$$

solutions.title: Partial fractions
solutions.body:
For $x\ne\pm1$,
$$\frac{x}{x^2-1}=\frac12\left(\frac{1}{x+1}+\frac{1}{x-1}\right),$$
since $\frac{1}{x+1}+\frac{1}{x-1}=\frac{(x-1)+(x+1)}{x^2-1}=\frac{2x}{x^2-1}$.

For any constant $c$, induction on $n$ gives
$$\frac{d^n}{dx^n}\,(x-c)^{-1}=(-1)(-2)\cdots(-n)\,(x-c)^{-1-n}=\frac{(-1)^n\,n!}{(x-c)^{n+1}} .$$
Applying this with $c=-1$ and $c=1$:
$$f^{(n)}(x)=\frac{(-1)^n\,n!}{2}\left(\frac{1}{(x+1)^{n+1}}+\frac{1}{(x-1)^{n+1}}\right),\qquad x\ne\pm1 .$$

**Check ($n=1$):** the formula gives $-\frac12\left(\frac1{(x+1)^2}+\frac1{(x-1)^2}\right)=-\frac{x^2+1}{(x^2-1)^2}$, and indeed by the quotient rule $f'(x)=\frac{(x^2-1)-2x^2}{(x^2-1)^2}=-\frac{x^2+1}{(x^2-1)^2}$. ∎

solutions.title: Leibniz rule on $(x^2-1)f(x)=x$
solutions.body:
Differentiate the identity $(x^2-1)f(x)=x$ $n$ times with the Leibniz rule (for $n\ge2$ the right side gives $0$):
$$(x^2-1)f^{(n)}+2nx\,f^{(n-1)}+n(n-1)f^{(n-2)}=0 .$$
This recursion, with $f$ and $f'$ known, determines all derivatives. One checks that
$g_n(x)=\frac{(-1)^n n!}{2}\left((x+1)^{-n-1}+(x-1)^{-n-1}\right)$ satisfies it: writing $g_n=\frac{(-1)^nn!}2(A^{n+1}+B^{n+1})$ with $A=\frac1{x+1}$, $B=\frac1{x-1}$, the terms in $A$ give
$$\tfrac{(-1)^{n}}{2}A^{n+1}\Big[n!(x^2-1)-2n\cdot(n-1)!\,x(x+1)+n(n-1)(n-2)!\,(x+1)^2\Big]=\tfrac{(-1)^{n}n!}{2}A^{n+1}(x+1)\Big[(x-1)-2x+(x+1)\Big]=0,$$
and the terms in $B$ vanish the same way. Since $g_0=f$ and $g_1=f'$, induction gives $f^{(n)}=g_n$ for all $n$, the same formula as before. ∎

prompt:
Prove that there exist two real convex functions $f,g$ such that
$$f(x)-g(x)=\sin x$$
for all $x\in\mathbb R$.

solutions.title: Add a strongly convex function
solutions.body:
Let
$$f(x)=x^2+\sin x,\qquad g(x)=x^2 .$$
Clearly $f(x)-g(x)=\sin x$ for every real $x$. Both functions are twice differentiable on $\mathbb R$ with
$$f''(x)=2-\sin x\ge 1>0,\qquad g''(x)=2>0,$$
and a twice differentiable function with nonnegative second derivative on an interval is convex there. Hence $f$ and $g$ are convex. ∎

solutions.title: A general principle
solutions.body:
More generally, if $h$ is twice differentiable with $|h''|\le K$, then $h=\big(h+\tfrac K2x^2\big)-\tfrac K2x^2$ is a difference of two convex functions, since $\big(h+\tfrac K2x^2\big)''=h''+K\ge0$. For $h=\sin x$ we have $|h''|=|\sin x|\le1$, so even
$$f(x)=\sin x+\tfrac12x^2,\qquad g(x)=\tfrac12x^2$$
works ($f''=1-\sin x\ge0$). ∎

answer: Modulo $n-1$ we have $n\equiv1$, so $n^n-n^2+n-1\equiv1-1+1-1=0$ (equivalently: $x=1$ is a root of $x^n-x^2+x-1$).

solutions.title: Factor theorem
solutions.body:
Fix an integer $n>1$ and consider the polynomial with integer coefficients
$$P(x)=x^n-x^2+x-1 .$$
$P(1)=1-1+1-1=0$, so by the factor theorem $P(x)=(x-1)Q(x)$, and since $x-1$ is monic, $Q$ has integer coefficients (polynomial long division by a monic polynomial never creates fractions). Substituting $x=n$:
$$n^n-n^2+n-1=(n-1)\,Q(n),\qquad Q(n)\in\mathbb Z,$$
so $(n-1)\mid n^n-n^2+n-1$. ∎

solutions.title: Congruences
solutions.body:
Let $m=n-1\ge1$. Then $n\equiv 1\pmod m$, hence $n^k\equiv1\pmod m$ for every $k\ge0$ (products of congruences). Therefore
$$n^n-n^2+n-1\equiv 1-1+1-1=0\pmod m ,$$
i.e. $n-1$ divides $n^n-n^2+n-1$. (For $n=2$, $m=1$ divides everything, and indeed $4-4+2-1=1$.) ∎

prompt: Let $X$ be a finite set and $f\colon X\to X$ be a map. Prove that $f$ is an injective map if and only if $f$ is a surjective map.
answer: With $|X|=n$: injective $\Rightarrow$ $|f(X)|=n$ $\Rightarrow$ $f(X)=X$; surjective $\Rightarrow$ the $n$ fibres $f^{-1}(y)$ are nonempty, disjoint and cover $n$ elements, so each has exactly one element.

solutions.title: Counting
solutions.body:
Let $|X|=n$ (if $X=\emptyset$ there is nothing to prove). For $y\in X$ let $f^{-1}(y)=\{x\in X: f(x)=y\}$ be the fibre over $y$. The fibres are pairwise disjoint and their union is $X$, so
$$\sum_{y\in X}\big|f^{-1}(y)\big|=n.\tag{$*$}$$

**Injective $\Rightarrow$ surjective.** If $f$ is injective, distinct elements have distinct images, so the image $f(X)$ has exactly $n$ elements. It is a subset of the $n$-element set $X$, hence $f(X)=X$: $f$ is surjective.

**Surjective $\Rightarrow$ injective.** If $f$ is surjective, each of the $n$ fibres is nonempty, i.e. $|f^{-1}(y)|\ge1$. By $(*)$ the $n$ numbers $|f^{-1}(y)|\ge1$ add up to $n$, so each equals $1$. Thus every $y$ has exactly one preimage, which means $f$ is injective. ∎

(Finiteness is essential: on $\mathbb N$, $n\mapsto n+1$ is injective but not surjective, and $n\mapsto\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ is surjective but not injective.)
